If you are AGI-pilled, a capability maximalist, an x-risk person, etc. this data has to move you at some point, right?

https://t.co/U5f3D9zMrQ

Slow diffusion can only be part of the story, esp. given such muted employment / productivity effects in coding as late as this spring (see: https://t.co/rkfmrqvRVn).

IMO everyone should be thinking more about the variety of structural limitations faced by LLMs, things like hallucination, reward-hacking, context rot, insufficient data esp. outside of math/SWE, poor generalization, unpredictability (same prompt, different outputs), user-sensitivity (output quality is a function of use quality), mode collapse (model outputs lack humanlike diversity), the uncodifiability of much of humans' load-bearing tacit knowledge, and cultural stigma/anti-inductive norms (AI outputs become cheap, low-status baselines).

One red flag for me in a lot of maximalist AI discourse is the assumption that models being (in some sense) intelligent, and their becoming more intelligent, licenses any and all inferences about what they might do. This is similar to the oft-made "intelligence-as-magic" objection.

The problem here is that there are many different kinds of intelligence, with unique powers and limitations, and the wider world can relate to each one in different ways. I have yet to encounter a serious attempt to characterize the unique KIND of intelligence LLMs have.

The more I think about it, the more I think that the term "artificial intelligence" may be part of the problem here, and that it would actually be less misleading in certain respects to construe LLMs as "artificial organisms" or "lifeforms."

This has its own risks of course, but if nothing else it cuts against the impression that LLMs are ethereal demigods on the road to full omniscience, and suggests instead that they are more like animals with a set of capacities we can come to constrain and understand. It could also help us better explore their strange variety of distributed silicon embodiment, and the related fact that they need to consume scarce resources to survive.

This picture seems closer to the truth to me.

Company idea - Instinct for healthcare workers

It’s clear to me that people are going to try to use personal AI tools like Instinct to do things at their job. Does your job require you to get data from different places and fill out a lot of forms? Or send a lot of follow up emails, etc.? Or make updates to various google docs where you lowkey don’t know where that doc even lives? 

This tool is EXTREMELY tempting to use for that because it’s excellent at that.

However this is also a security and privacy nightmare. These personal AI tools can basically mimic you as they go through your systems which is what makes them useful but also very scary. It even knows to switch to a YouTube short for like 10 seconds before switching back to the task at hand. 

So any company that touches PHI, or sensitive data has to watch out because these tools will find it and accidentally expose it.

But again because it’s such a useful tool for employees you are 100% going to have people trying to use it for work at healthcare companies. So your options are:

1) Do your best to fight it and put in internal security that watches for actions that look bot-ish. However that takes internal resources and will always be an arms race against the personal AI tools that find workarounds.

2) Create compliant paths/tools that work like personal AI tools but have the appropriate security/privacy guardrails.

There’s probably opportunity in both of these buckets, but I’m more interested in the second. Something like an agent that gets its own login and virtual desktop on the org’s network instead of impersonating with cached passwords, the brain can be a cloud model under a BAA, memory is maintained locally, etc. Each employee’s agent gets different permissions/requirements of human-in-the-loop depending on their role.

There are some seedlings of companies attempting to do this. Contxt is one for regular enterprises, Heidi’s new agent is more healthcare specific. But there is a lot more to be done here and probably could be more specific to different roles in healthcare (e.g. Instinct for clinical research coordinators).

I have been trying to use AI agents to transact on @zomato, @Uber_India and @letsblinkit. Lots of friction. Until agents can show these marketplaces' catalogs and inventory as generative UI, user experience will be far from ideal. 

My bet: horizontal personal agents will win the long tail / low-frequency use cases, like buying insurance, an obscure brand, or a chair etc

But every high-frequency apps like ride-hailing, food, fashion etc will have its own agent on @WhatsApp. 

In the mobile era, you had a home screen full of apps. In the AI era, you will have a WhatsApp full of agents.
